nameStory: This millipede doesn't have a widely-used common name, so it goes by its scientific name Craspedosoma rawlinsii. The genus name Craspedosoma comes from Greek words meaning 'fringed body,' likely referring to the delicate, segmented appearance of these tiny millipedes. The species name honors someone named Rawlins, though the exact person is lost to scientific history.
description: Craspedosoma rawlinsii is a tiny millipede that's barely bigger than your pinky nail, reaching only about 16mm (roughly 2/3 of an inch) in length. This delicate creature has 30 distinct body segments, giving it a segmented, worm-like appearance as it slowly crawls through leaf litter. Unlike centipedes which are fast predators, millipedes like this one are gentle decomposers that help break down dead plant material. Though native to Europe, this little millipede has somehow made its way to North America and occasionally turns up in New England.

idTips.label: Size and segments
idTips.description: Extremely small at only 16mm long with exactly 30 visible body segments that you can count if you look closely with a magnifying glass

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Moves very slowly in a gentle, wave-like motion, unlike the quick darting movements of centipedes

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Cylindrical and worm-like with a smooth, slightly shiny surface that feels firm but not hard when gently touched

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Two pairs of tiny legs per body segment, creating a rippling motion as it walks - too small to count easily without magnification

idTips.label: Coiling behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, curls into a tight spiral or partial coil, remaining motionless until the threat passes

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Found in moist leaf litter and decaying wood where it feeds on decomposing plant matter

habitat: Look for this tiny millipede in moist, rich leaf litter under deciduous trees, particularly in areas with deep organic soil layers. It prefers cool, humid microhabitats like the underside of rotting logs, beneath thick leaf mats, or in compost-rich soil around old tree stumps. Since it's an introduced European species with very few New England records, finding one would be quite remarkable and worth documenting.

seasonality.spring: Most active as soil warms and moisture levels are high from snowmelt. Look under freshly fallen logs or in areas where last year's leaves are beginning to decompose.
seasonality.summer: Retreats deeper into soil or under thicker cover during hot, dry periods. Best found in consistently moist areas during early morning or after rain.
seasonality.fall: May become more visible again as temperatures cool and autumn rains increase soil moisture. Active in fresh leaf litter as it begins to break down.
seasonality.winter: Likely dormant deep in soil or under thick insulating layers of organic matter. Nearly impossible to find during cold months.

funFact: This tiny millipede is basically a living European immigrant that somehow crossed the Atlantic Ocean - with only 2 recorded sightings in all of New England, you're more likely to spot a rare bird than encounter one of these microscopic travelers!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other tiny millipedes or even small earthworm segments, but the key difference is the distinct segmentation and tiny legs. Remember: millipedes have two pairs of legs per segment and move slowly, while centipedes have one pair per segment and move quickly. Young earthworms lack the obvious segmentation and have no visible legs at all.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the more mysterious aspects of modern ecology - how European soil invertebrates occasionally show up in North American gardens and forests, likely transported accidentally in soil, plants, or organic matter. With only 2 New England records, any sighting should be photographed and reported to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Since this is the only Craspedosoma species recorded in New England, compare it with other small millipedes in the region by counting segments (this one has exactly 30) and noting its extremely small size. Most other New England millipedes are either much larger or have different segment counts, making this species quite distinctive despite its tiny stature.
